title: UNIT 7: CONTEMPORARY GEOGRAPHICAL ISSUES — DESERTIFICATION AND LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Contemporary geographical issues → important problems and challenges of the present time that have geographical dimensions and affect people, places and the environment.

These issues can be understood by examining where they occur, how they change through time, and how human activities interact with the natural environment.

Desertification and land degradation are important contemporary geographical issues because they affect natural resources, agricultural production, livelihoods and the environment.

title: 7.1 INTRODUCTION TO CONTEMPORARY GEOGRAPHICAL ISSUES
notes:
Contemporary issues → problems or challenges that exist in the present period and have significant effects on people, places and the environment.

◆ GEOGRAPHICAL DIMENSIONS OF CONTEMPORARY ISSUES
✓ Spatial dimension → considers where an issue occurs, its geographical distribution, and differences between places.
✓ Temporal dimension → considers how an issue develops, changes and persists over time.
✓ Human-environment dimension → examines the relationship between human activities and the natural environment.

Contemporary geographical issues are not isolated from one another. A problem in one place can affect other places through environmental, economic and social connections.

◆ HUMAN AGENCY AND THE ENVIRONMENT
Human beings have a dual capacity in their relationship with the natural environment.

✓ Destructive capacity → human activities can damage or destroy ecosystems through deforestation, overgrazing, over-cultivation, pollution, excessive resource use and inappropriate land management.

✓ Restorative capacity → human beings can also protect and restore ecosystems through conservation, afforestation, sustainable agriculture, soil and water conservation, proper resource management and rehabilitation of degraded land.

Therefore, human activities can either accelerate environmental degradation or contribute to environmental recovery and sustainable resource use.

title: 7.2 DESERTIFICATION AND DRYLANDS
notes:
Desert → a naturally occurring dry area characterized by very low precipitation and limited vegetation.

Desertification → land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities.

Desertification does not mean the natural expansion of existing deserts. It refers to the degradation of productive land in dryland areas.

◆ DRYLANDS
Drylands → areas where water availability is limited because precipitation is low compared with potential evaporation and plant water requirements.

Drylands include:

✓ Arid areas → very dry areas with very limited rainfall and vegetation.
✓ Semi-arid areas → areas receiving more rainfall than arid areas but still having significant water limitations.
✓ Dry sub-humid areas → areas that receive more rainfall than semi-arid areas but can still experience seasonal water shortages and land degradation.

◆ PHYSICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF DRYLANDS
✓ Low and highly variable rainfall.
✓ High rates of evaporation.
✓ Water scarcity or seasonal water shortages.
✓ Sparse and uneven vegetation in many areas.
✓ Soils that can be vulnerable to erosion and degradation when vegetation cover is removed.
✓ High sensitivity to climatic variability and prolonged drought.

Drylands support large populations and important economic activities, including crop production, livestock rearing and other forms of natural-resource use. Their resources therefore need careful management.

title: 7.3 CAUSES OF DESERTIFICATION
notes:
Desertification results from the interaction of natural and human factors. Human activities can greatly increase the pressure placed on already fragile dryland environments.

◆ RAPID POPULATION GROWTH
Rapid population growth → an increase in the number of people within a given area over time.

Rapid population growth can increase demand for:
✓ Agricultural land.
✓ Grazing land.
✓ Fuelwood and other forest products.
✓ Water resources.
✓ Food and other natural resources.

As resource demand increases, land may be cultivated or grazed more intensively, forests may be cleared, and the natural vegetation cover may decline.

◆ OVERGRAZING
Overgrazing → excessive grazing of vegetation by livestock beyond the ability of the vegetation and soil to recover.

Overgrazing can:
✓ Remove protective vegetation cover.
✓ Expose soil to wind and water erosion.
✓ Reduce soil fertility.
✓ Prevent natural vegetation from recovering.
✓ Reduce the productivity of grazing land.

◆ OVER-CULTIVATION
Over-cultivation → continuous or excessive cultivation of land without allowing sufficient time for the soil to recover.

It can cause:
✓ Depletion of soil nutrients.
✓ Loss of soil organic matter.
✓ Soil erosion.
✓ Declining agricultural productivity.
✓ Increased vulnerability of land to degradation.

◆ DEFORESTATION
Deforestation → the removal or clearing of forests and trees without adequate replacement or regeneration.

Deforestation contributes to desertification by:
✓ Removing vegetation that protects the soil.
✓ Increasing soil erosion.
✓ Reducing soil moisture retention.
✓ Destroying habitats and reducing biodiversity.
✓ Increasing pressure on already fragile ecosystems.

◆ INADEQUATE AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES
Unsuitable farming practices can accelerate land degradation, particularly where environmental conditions are fragile.

✓ Lack of proper crop rotation → repeatedly growing the same crop or failing to rotate crops can contribute to nutrient depletion and declining soil quality.

✓ Insufficient fallow period → failing to allow cultivated land enough time to recover naturally can reduce soil fertility and increase degradation.

✓ Continuous cultivation → cultivating land repeatedly without adequate recovery can exhaust soil nutrients and increase erosion.

◆ CLIMATIC FACTORS
Drought and climatic variability can contribute to land degradation, particularly when combined with human pressure.

Drought → a prolonged period of unusually low precipitation that results in water shortages.

When drought occurs in areas already affected by overgrazing, deforestation or over-cultivation, vegetation recovery becomes more difficult and desertification may intensify.

title: 7.4 IMPACTS OF DESERTIFICATION AND LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Land degradation → the decline in the quality, productivity and productive capacity of land as a result of natural processes or human activities.

Desertification and land degradation produce environmental, economic and social consequences.

◆ ENVIRONMENTAL CONSEQUENCES
✓ Soil erosion → removal of fertile topsoil by water or wind.
✓ Loss of vegetation cover → reduction of plants that protect soil and support ecosystems.
✓ Loss of biodiversity → reduction in the variety of plants, animals and other organisms.
✓ Declining soil fertility → reduction in the ability of soil to support plant growth.
✓ Reduced land productivity → decline in the amount of agricultural or grazing production obtained from land.
✓ Water-resource degradation → increased sedimentation and reduced quality of water resources.
✓ Habitat destruction → loss or deterioration of habitats required by plants and animals.

◆ SOCIO-ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES
✓ Food insecurity → inadequate or uncertain access to sufficient food.
✓ Declining agricultural production → degradation reduces the ability of land to produce crops and livestock feed.
✓ Poverty → reduced agricultural productivity and natural-resource availability can reduce household income and increase vulnerability.
✓ Loss of livelihoods → people who depend on farming, livestock and other natural resources may lose their sources of income.
✓ Migration → environmental and economic pressures can encourage people to move temporarily or permanently to other areas.
✓ Increased competition for resources → scarcity of productive land, water and grazing resources can increase competition among users.

◆ EFFECT ON RURAL COMMUNITIES
People whose livelihoods depend heavily on agriculture and livestock are particularly vulnerable to land degradation. Declining land productivity can reduce food production and income, making households more vulnerable to poverty and food insecurity.

title: 7.5 THE VICIOUS CYCLE OF DESERTIFICATION
notes:
Desertification can form a vicious cycle in which environmental degradation and human poverty reinforce one another.

◆ VICIOUS CYCLE
Population pressure → increased demand for land and natural resources → over-cultivation, overgrazing and deforestation → removal of vegetation cover → soil erosion and declining soil fertility → reduced land productivity → lower agricultural production and income → food insecurity and poverty → increased dependence on natural resources → further pressure on land → continued degradation.

This cycle shows that desertification is not only an environmental problem. It can also become a social and economic problem.

Poverty may increase dependence on land, forests and grazing resources, while declining environmental productivity can make it more difficult for people to escape poverty.

◆ MIGRATION AND DESERTIFICATION
When land can no longer provide sufficient food, employment or income, people may migrate to other rural areas, towns or cities.

Migration can reduce pressure on a degraded area in some cases, but it can also create additional pressure on the resources and services of receiving areas.

title: KEY TERMS OF UNIT 7
notes:
Contemporary geographical issue → a present-day problem or challenge with important spatial, temporal and human-environment dimensions.

Desert → a naturally dry environment with very low precipitation and limited vegetation.

Desertification → land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities.

Dryland → an area characterized by limited water availability and including arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid zones.

Overgrazing → grazing livestock beyond the capacity of vegetation and land to recover.

Over-cultivation → excessive or continuous cultivation that does not allow sufficient recovery of soil.

Deforestation → removal or clearing of forests and trees.

Drought → a prolonged period of unusually low precipitation causing water shortages.

Land degradation → decline in the quality and productive capacity of land.

Soil erosion → removal of soil by agents such as water and wind.

Food insecurity → inadequate or uncertain access to sufficient and nutritious food.

Vicious cycle → a process in which one problem causes another, which in turn reinforces the original problem.
